title: A ten-year correction reduced later butterfly growth prediction error, but its added climate gain was uncertain
abstract: We tested whether calibration can explain failure of old climate models. We used published annual predictions from models fitted through 1994. We fitted a slope and mean correction in 1995-2004 and tested it in 2005-2024. For 32 UK butterfly growth units, the skill against the original baseline changed from -53.8% to +14.1%. The gain against a baseline with its own mean correction was 7.1%. A test-year block interval was 4.6-9.6%. When calibration years were also resampled, the interval crossed zero in 31 complete units. The fixed five-term weather model gave no added gain. Swiss spring and later plant dates retained large gains under calibration resampling. Butterfly flight dates gave a small uncertain gain against the corrected baseline. Thus, original model failure can contain a correctable signal, but a ten-year record did not establish a reliable growth correction. This is a retrospective analysis of prior data, not independent field validation. Short records, fixed source fits, changing surveys and observed-weather inputs limit inference. Code, aggregate results, figures, hashes and reproduction instructions are included.
